hero.title: Play, powered by robotics.
hero.subtitle: GEarheads brings hands-on STEM activities to patients at Children's Wisconsin, built on play-therapy research. Four seasons in, we're still the hospital's only ongoing FIRST program.

impact.label: Why it matters
impact.text: Dr. Jeffrey Karst's research found that purposeful activity helps kids recover. We built this program around that — every activity aims for a moment of focus or a small win. Four seasons and 21 sessions later, we're still the only FTC team with a standing program here, working year-round with Child Life.

statsAllTime.label: Total Sessions
statsAllTime.hint: The longest-running FIRST program at the hospital

activities.label: Paper Circuits
activities.tagline: When a drawing lights up, it changes everything.
activities.description: Patients lay copper tape onto paper, add an LED and a coin-cell battery, and watch their drawing light up. No fine motor skills needed — the tape forgives an imperfect path. We keep it simple: a circuit just needs a complete loop.
highlights: Patients light up their own artwork
No electronics background needed
Works one-handed or with limited motion
Shows voltage and circuits firsthand
Early finishers try multiple LEDs

activities.label: Catapults
activities.tagline: Engineering the perfect launch — one rubber band at a time.
activities.description: Patients build a mini catapult from craft sticks, rubber bands, and a spoon, then aim it at a target. Every miss becomes data — too much tension, arm too short. Our students ask questions instead of giving answers, so patients find the fix themselves.
highlights: Patients build, launch, and improve their catapult
Shows tension and motion through trial and error
Works bedside, on a tray table
Students coach, don't just assemble
Older patients can graph launch distance

activities.label: Pneumatic Machines
activities.tagline: Compressed air, piston motion, and a real mechanism in your hands.
activities.description: Patients build a small pneumatic mechanism — tubing, a syringe, a valve — and use it to push, lift, or clamp something. Air pushed into a sealed space has to go somewhere, so it moves the piston. We tie that to how our robot uses pneumatics to grab game pieces.
highlights: Hands-on mechanism with tubing and a valve
Shows pressure and force in real time
Ties to how our robot uses pneumatics
Safe for all ages, no sharp edges
Fast feedback keeps sessions engaging

activities.label: Robotics Kits
activities.tagline: Build a robot. Program it. Drive it.
activities.description: For patients with more time, we bring FLL and SPIKE Prime kits — the same hardware from our veterans program. Patients build a small LEGO robot, then block-code it through a course. We scale it to the patient: a young child just programs a stop; an older one adds a turn or sensor. A full build fits in 30–45 minutes.
highlights: FLL and SPIKE Prime — real competition hardware
Students adapt the build to each patient's pace
Block-coding — no typing or syntax errors
Build-to-drive in 30–45 minutes
Older patients add sensors or loops

activities.label: Live FTC Demo
activities.tagline: This is what all the building leads to.
activities.description: At the high point of every session, we bring our full-size robot, Gearboticus, into the hospital and let patients drive it. Thirty-plus pounds, full competition speed, scoring on its own in under 30 seconds — nothing else compares. We explain each system, intake to flywheel, at whatever level fits the patient.
highlights: Full-scale robot on the floor, not a video
Patients drive Gearboticus from a real driver station
Technical depth adjusted to each patient
Ties every earlier activity to real robotics
Students explain their choices simply

activities.label: Leave-Behind Kits
activities.tagline: So the session continues after we leave.
activities.description: Hospital stays mean long stretches between activities. We put together leave-behind kits — copper tape, LEDs, craft sticks, a challenge card — so patients keep experimenting after we leave, no screen or adult needed. They also give family something to do together, which Child Life says matters.
highlights: Lets patients keep experimenting after we leave
Copper tape, LEDs, craft sticks, challenge cards
Self-explanatory — no screen needed
Gives family something to do together
Assembled in bulk before every visit

delivery.label: How We Deliver
delivery.heading: Hybrid delivery — wherever patients are
delivery.subtext: Not every patient can leave their room. Livestream and video let us reach them too.

modes.title: In-Person Sessions
modes.desc: Students visit Children's Wisconsin with materials and the full FTC robot. Sessions run in the hospital's activity space, with someone at every table.

modes.title: Livestream
modes.desc: Patients who can't leave their room join live, on an in-room screen, watching the activity and our students up close.

modes.title: WeVideo Tutorials
modes.desc: Short videos covering materials, steps, and troubleshooting, so anyone can run an activity on their own, anytime.

modes.title: Lights & Motion STEM Kits
modes.desc: Child Life can hand these out between visits — kits we developed together for self-guided STEM, no team visit required.
